body.heading: Overwhelm is a traffic jam of tasks
paragraphs: Overwhelm usually is not one enormous problem. It is many problems arriving at once, all shouting, until the mind cannot rank them and freezes. From inside the freeze, people often conclude they are incapable. In fact the ranking system is just overloaded.
The way out is not to solve the whole pile. It is to pick one item — almost any item — and let motion return.

body.heading: How to choose the next thing
paragraphs: Ask: what is the next physical action, small enough to do in the next ten minutes, that would make anything better? Send the email that unblocks three people. Wash the one plate. Write the first sentence. Book the appointment. The best next thing is usually obvious once you demand it be tiny and physical.

If even choosing feels impossible, use the body’s list first: water, food, daylight, movement, sleep. A surprising number of “everything is impossible” moments are actually “I am running on empty” moments wearing a disguise.

body.heading: One thing, then reassess
paragraphs: After the next right thing, pause and look again. The pile has not vanished, but it has changed shape, and so have you: you are now a person in motion with one fewer open loop. Choose the next thing from there.
This is a modest method, and that is its strength. It asks nothing heroic of you on the days you feel least heroic. It just asks for one right thing — and then, when you are ready, another.

takeaway: Do not solve the whole pile. Do the next right thing, then look again.
